title: Autism, anxiety and sensory overload
blurb: Recognise anxiety and sensory overload in autistic people and adjust the environment and routine before distress builds.
question: Tyler, 20, is autistic and has a learning disability. On a busy medical ward he covers his ears, rocks and then hits the wall when the meal trolley arrives. What should the nurse do first, and how can the next few days be made more predictable?

teach.body: Many autistic people experience sensory input differently: noise, light, touch and smell can feel far stronger. Unexpected change and uncertainty also drive anxiety. When demands and sensory input build up faster than the person can cope, distress follows. In plain English: the ward is not 'just noisy' for Tyler, it may be overwhelming. NICE asks staff to adjust the environment and give predictable, visual information as reasonable adjustments, rather than expecting the person to adapt alone.

steps.label: Early signs
steps.sub: Covering ears, pacing, rocking, repeating words

teach.caption: Acting at the early-signs stage prevents most crises. Learn each person's signs from family and the hospital passport.

teach.body: The National Autistic Society describes a meltdown as an intense response to an overwhelming situation, in which the person temporarily loses control of their behaviour. It is not naughty or attention-seeking. Some people instead withdraw, go quiet or stop responding. Either way, the response is to reduce input and demands, keep everyone safe, speak little and calmly, and give time. Questions, touch and crowding usually add to the overload.

They often occur together on a ward; plan for both.

items: Read the hospital passport and ask family what calms and what upsets the person.
Book a side room or quiet bay, away from alarms and the nurses' station.
Prepare a visual schedule of the day and photos of the ward and key staff.
Offer the first or last slot to cut waiting time.
Agree in advance who will explain each procedure and how.

teach.h: Scenario: Tyler on the medical ward
teach.body: The nurse notices Tyler covering his ears as the trolley rattles in: an early sign. She reduces input first: she moves him to a quieter side room, dims the lights and asks staff to speak one at a time. She does not question him while he is distressed. Once calm, she works with his mother to create a photo board of who is on shift and a picture timetable for meals and observations. The episodes stop because the triggers were removed, not because Tyler was told to behave.

teach.text: Classic error: treating distress as 'behaviour' to be managed with PRN sedation or restraint. NICE says do not use antipsychotics, antidepressants or anticonvulsants for the core features of autism, and reactive strategies are a last resort. First ask: what in the environment or routine is causing this?

teach.caption: A memory aid for this app, not an official tool.

items: Sensory differences and unexpected change are common drivers of distress in autistic people.
Spot early signs and reduce input before overload.
A meltdown is an overwhelmed response, not a tantrum; withdrawal is another form.
NICE adjustments: visual supports, personal space, lighting, noise, colours, first or last appointment.
Anxiety disorders also co-occur with autism and need proper assessment (NG54 1.7.4).

summary: You can now recognise early signs of anxiety and sensory overload in autistic people and respond by reducing input and demands. You can plan predictable, visual, low-stimulus care as the reasonable adjustments NICE describes.

A.q: Jacob, 26, is autistic and has a moderate learning disability. During a fire alarm test at his day service he stops talking, sits on the floor and does not respond to staff. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask him clear, simple questions to check his level of consciousness
Guide him gently to a quiet area and give him time to recover
Hold his hands firmly to stop him rocking and reassure him
Call 999 because he is not responding to verbal prompts
A.why: Withdrawal after overwhelming sensory input can be a shutdown response. Reducing stimulation, staying calmly nearby and allowing time is the right response.

whyNot.0: Repeated questions add demands and input to a person who is already overloaded.
whyNot.2: Touch and holding can intensify overload and may be restraint that is not justified here.
whyNot.3: The context explains his reduced response; there are no signs of a medical emergency.

A.q: Maya, 17, is autistic. Her clinic has moved to a new room at short notice and she becomes very anxious in the waiting area. Which adjustment would most help at her next appointment?
options: A longer wait so she can get used to the new room
Booking her in the middle of the afternoon clinic
Advance notice of the change with a photo of the room
Seeing her with several staff so that help is close at hand
A.why: Unexpected change commonly drives anxiety. Advance warning and visual information make the change predictable (CG170 1.1.9 visual supports).

whyNot.0: Waiting increases anxiety; CG170 1.1.10 suggests minimising waiting time.
whyNot.1: CG170 1.1.10 suggests the start or end of the day, when waiting is shortest.
whyNot.3: More people adds sensory and social demand.

A.q: A healthcare assistant asks why the nurse is changing the lighting and moving the bed of Ravi, 30, who is autistic, rather than asking the doctor for a sedative. Which explanation is best?
options: Environmental adjustment is a first step that NICE recommends
Sedation is reserved for people who are over 65 years old
Lighting changes are a cheaper option than prescribing
Ravi has refused sedatives in the past and so cannot have them
A.why: For autistic adults NICE CG142 1.1.8 recommends adjusting the environment (lighting, noise, personal space), and 1.5.1 says address environmental triggers before other interventions; medicines are not used for core features of autism (CG142 1.4.21-1.4.22).

whyNot.1: Age is not the reason; medication is not the first response to sensory distress at any age.
whyNot.2: Cost is not the clinical rationale for the adjustment.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the scenario says he refused; the reason is that the environment is the cause.

B.q: Aiden, 34, is autistic and has a learning disability. He is due to be admitted next week for dental treatment under general anaesthetic. Which preparation is most likely to reduce his anxiety on the day?
options: Explaining the plan verbally to him on arrival at the unit
A visual schedule of the day agreed with Aiden and his carers
Admitting him the evening before so that he can settle overnight
Asking his carers not to tell him until the morning itself
B.why: Visual supports prepared in advance with the person and carers make the day predictable (CG142 1.1.8 visual supports for autistic adults; Equality Act anticipatory adjustments).

whyNot.0: Verbal explanation on arrival gives no time to prepare and may not be understood under stress.
whyNot.2: A night in an unfamiliar ward adds change and sensory load.
whyNot.3: Withholding information removes predictability and can increase distress.

B.q: Isla, 15, is autistic. Her parents report she now avoids school, has stomach aches every morning and lies awake worrying. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: These are core autistic traits that need no further action
These signs are typical of teenage behaviour and are likely to pass
This suggests a learning disability that was missed earlier
These may show a co-occurring anxiety problem needing assessment
B.why: Anxiety commonly co-occurs with autism and can present with physical symptoms and avoidance. NICE CG170 names coexisting anxiety as a problem to assess (1.4.1) and treat, for example with adapted CBT (1.7.2).

whyNot.0: Putting new worry and avoidance down to autism itself is diagnostic overshadowing; a change needs assessment.
whyNot.1: Daily physical symptoms, sleepless worry and school avoidance are not a passing teenage phase and need assessment.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests impaired general intellect; the picture is anxiety.

B.q: Ravi, 30, is autistic and in hospital after a fall. He becomes distressed each morning when unfamiliar staff arrive. The ward cannot guarantee the same staff every day. What is the best adjustment?
options: Ask his family to stay every morning in place of staff
Offer PRN lorazepam at the start of each morning shift
Use a photo board each morning showing who is caring for him
Move him to a different ward that has a smaller nursing team
B.why: The trigger is unpredictability. If staff cannot be constant (CG142 1.1.4 asks for continuity wherever possible), making the change predictable with visual information is the next best adjustment (CG142 1.1.8 visual supports).

whyNot.0: Families can help, but replacing staff care is not a fair or reliable adjustment.
whyNot.1: Medication does not address the cause and is not a first response to distress from change.
whyNot.3: A ward move is a bigger change and would increase distress.

C.q: Tyler, 20, is autistic with a learning disability. On a busy ward he covers his ears and rocks as the meal trolley arrives, then hits the wall. A healthcare assistant suggests asking for PRN haloperidol. What is the most appropriate initial action?
options: Request the PRN medicine as the behaviour poses a risk
Hold his arms to prevent injury until he calms down
Explain the ward rules to him clearly and firmly
Reduce noise and move him to a quieter side room
C.why: His signs point to sensory overload from the trolley noise. Reducing input and moving to a quieter space addresses the cause, as NICE recommends; medicines are not used for core features of autism.

whyNot.0: Medication does not remove the trigger; NICE advises against drugs for core autistic features and reactive strategies are a last resort.
whyNot.1: Physical holding adds sensory input and is restraint without clear necessity.
whyNot.2: Verbal demands increase overload while he is distressed.

C.q: Chloe, 22, is autistic and has a moderate learning disability. She needs a blood test but became very distressed at previous attempts. Her mother says Chloe copes better with things she has practised. What is the best plan?
options: Gradual desensitisation, practice visits and a quiet planned slot
Book the test in a busy walk-in clinic so it is over with quickly
Ask several staff to hold her so that the sample is taken safely
Take the blood while she is asleep without telling her
C.why: Planned, gradual desensitisation and a quiet first or last slot are reasonable adjustments that reduce anxiety and respect her rights.

whyNot.1: A busy walk-in clinic adds waiting, noise and crowding, the sensory load that CG142 1.1.8 asks staff to reduce.
whyNot.2: Restraint for a planned test is not the least restrictive option.
whyNot.3: Covert procedures need a lawful capacity and best interests basis and ignore less restrictive options.

C.q: Bella, 28, is autistic. On the ward she flaps her hands and hums when anxious. A student nurse plans to tell her to stop because 'it disturbs other patients'. Bella is not harming herself or others. What should the registered nurse advise?
options: Ask her to stop and offer a reward when she manages it
Allow it, as it may help her regulate in a stressful place
Move her to a single room so others are not disturbed
Record it as a new behaviour and make a referral to psychiatry
C.why: Repetitive movements and sounds often help autistic people manage anxiety and sensory input. Stopping harmless self-regulation can increase distress; the focus is the stressful environment.

whyNot.0: Rewarding suppression of a harmless coping strategy can raise anxiety.
whyNot.2: Isolation for others' convenience is not person-centred unless she wants a quieter room.
whyNot.3: This is described as her usual response to anxiety, not new behaviour needing referral.

reteach.title: The full cup
reteach.question: Imagine each noise, light, change and question as water poured into a cup. What happens when it overflows, and what should staff do?

blocks.h: Empty the cup, do not shake it
blocks.body: Every trigger adds water. Early signs (covering ears, rocking, repeating) mean the cup is nearly full. When it overflows the person may have a meltdown or shut down. The fix is to stop pouring (less noise, fewer demands) and give time for the level to drop, not to add questions, touch or medication.

blocks.text: A distressed autistic person is not being 'difficult'. Ask what changed in the environment or routine before thinking about medication or restraint.

explain.body: Autistic people may be over- or under-sensitive to noise, light, touch, smell and taste. Busy wards are full of alarms, bright lights and strangers. Ask about sensory needs on admission and record them.

test.q: Which change to the ward environment best follows NICE autism guidance?
options: Placing the person near the nurses' station for watching
Brighter lighting so staff can observe the person easily
Regular staff rotation so the person meets the whole team
Attention to lighting, noise and personal space
test.why: CG142 1.1.8 (adults) and CG170 1.1.9 (under 19s) name visual supports, personal space and attention to lighting, noise and wall colours.

whyNot.0: The nurses' station is often the noisiest place on a ward.
whyNot.1: Bright light can add to sensory overload.

explain.body: Unexpected change is a strong trigger. Tell the person what will happen, when and who will do it, using pictures, photos and schedules. Warn in advance of changes.

test.q: What is the main purpose of a visual schedule for an autistic person on a ward?
options: To make the day predictable and reduce anxiety
To replace all spoken communication with pictures
To record staff tasks for the nursing handover
To reward the person for following the routine
test.why: Visual schedules show what will happen and when, which reduces uncertainty and anxiety.

whyNot.1: Pictures support speech; they are used alongside it.
whyNot.2: It is for the person, not a staff task list.
whyNot.3: It is information, not a reward system.

explain.body: During a meltdown or shutdown: keep everyone safe, reduce input, use few calm words, avoid touch and questions, and give time. Afterwards, look for the trigger and plan to prevent it.

test.q: An autistic man is having a meltdown in a corridor. Which staff action is most helpful?
options: Ask him repeatedly what is wrong so you can help
Clear the area, stay calm and give him time and space
Hold his shoulders firmly to show you are in control
Tell him he will lose a privilege if he does not stop now
test.why: Reducing input, keeping everyone safe and allowing time is the recommended response to overwhelm.

whyNot.2: Touch can intensify distress and may be unjustified restraint.
whyNot.3: Threats treat overload as deliberate misbehaviour.

explain.h: Medicines are not the answer to autism
explain.body: NICE: do not use antipsychotics, antidepressants or anticonvulsants for the core features of autism (CG170 1.3.2; CG142 1.4.13, 1.4.21-1.4.22). Antipsychotics for behaviour that challenges are considered by specialists, usually alongside psychosocial support, when other approaches have not worked or the behaviour is too severe for them to be delivered (CG142 1.5.7-1.5.8).

test.q: A doctor asks whether an antidepressant would reduce the core social communication difficulties of a 12-year-old autistic boy. What does NICE advise?
options: Use one if his behaviour has been difficult for a month
Use one alongside a sensory diet for best effect
Do not use antidepressants for core autistic features
Use one if the parents agree it is in his interests
test.why: CG170 1.3.2: do not use antipsychotics, antidepressants, anticonvulsants or exclusion diets for the core features of autism in children and young people.

whyNot.0: Duration of difficulty does not change the recommendation for core features.
whyNot.1: Combining with another approach does not make it recommended.
whyNot.3: Parental agreement does not make a non-recommended treatment appropriate.
